name: Design an Ephemeral Preview Environments Platform
intent: Give every pull request its own running copy of the product at its own web address, create it in under a minute, and make it disappear on its own so that it costs almost nothing.
finalIntro: One pull request from its first push to its merge.
prompt: Design a platform that gives each pull request its own isolated, temporary environment. A company has 400 engineers opening about 60 pull requests per day, and a product made of a dozen services and a database. Reviewers and testers should open a link on the pull request and see that branch running with realistic data, without disturbing each other or production, and the bill should not grow with every forgotten branch.
functional: Create an environment when a pull request is opened and update it on every push
Reach each environment at its own address, such as pr-482.preview.example.com
Give each environment realistic test data and its own database state
Delete the environment when the pull request is merged or closed
Put the link and the status on the pull request
nonFunctional: The first environment is usable within about a minute of opening the pull request, and a push updates it within a couple of minutes
Environments cannot read or change each other's data, and have no access to production secrets
One environment cannot take the resources of the others
Idle environments cost almost nothing, and nothing outlives its pull request for long
Hundreds of environments exist at once, so each must be small
A missed event must never leave an environment running forever

firstAttempt.text: One shared staging environment. Developers deploy their branch to it when they need to show it, taking turns, and reviewers open the staging address. The database is the staging database.
limits: Only one branch can be on staging at a time, so developers queue or overwrite each other's work
Everyone's test data lands in one database, so tests interfere and the data decays
A reviewer cannot see a branch that has been replaced, and cannot compare two branches side by side
A broken branch on staging blocks everyone, including the release
Giving each branch a full virtual machine instead would take ten minutes to create and cost money all month

steps.title: Create a namespace per pull request from an event
steps.problem: One staging environment makes branches take turns, and a virtual machine or a whole cluster for each branch is too slow to create and too costly to leave running.
steps.fix: Run all previews in one shared cluster and give each pull request a namespace, such as pr-482, which is a cheap boundary for names, permissions and quotas. The source host sends an event when a pull request is opened, updated, merged or closed. A controller receives it, and creates or updates the namespace by applying the same templates (charts or manifests) that production uses, with the image built by CI for that commit. The event is a request to reconcile: the controller compares what should exist with what exists and fixes the difference, so a repeated or late event does no harm.
steps.tradeoff: Creating an environment is applying a few dozen objects, not building machines, so it takes seconds plus the time to start the containers. Everything shares one cluster, so isolation between previews has to be built deliberately in the later steps.

steps.title: Route by subdomain through one wildcard entry point
steps.problem: A new address for every pull request cannot mean a new DNS record, load balancer and certificate each time, which would be slow and would hit provider limits.
steps.fix: Point *.preview.example.com at one load balancer in front of an ingress controller, with one wildcard certificate. The controller registers a route for each namespace, which maps the host name pr-482.preview.example.com to that namespace's front service. The ingress reads the Host header and forwards the request. Creating a route is a change of configuration inside the cluster that takes effect in seconds, and no public DNS or certificate call is made per pull request.
steps.tradeoff: An address is free and instant, and every environment looks like a real site over HTTPS. Browsers treat every subdomain as a separate origin, but cookies set for the parent domain are shared, so session cookies must be set for the exact host. Sign-in with an external provider needs one fixed callback address, so a shared auth proxy handles it and passes users back to the right preview.

steps.title: Share the base services, and isolate by name
steps.problem: A dozen services plus a database, a cache and a queue per pull request would be hundreds of containers and a database server each, which is too slow to start and too expensive.
steps.fix: Run only what the pull request changed as its own deployment, and use shared stable versions of the rest. Heavy stateful services are shared and divided by name. A single database server hosts one schema or database per preview, the cache uses a key prefix and the queue uses a virtual host named after the namespace. Third-party systems such as payments are replaced by sandboxes or fakes. The namespace holds the credentials for its own schema only.
steps.tradeoff: A preview needs a few containers and a schema, so starting is quick and 100 or more can coexist. Shared services mean a heavy test can slow neighbours, a change to the shared server version affects everyone, and a bug that depends on infrastructure rather than code may not show up in a preview.

steps.title: Seed each database from a snapshot, without production data
steps.problem: An empty database makes a preview useless, but copying a production-size database for each pull request takes hours and puts customer data where it must not be.
steps.fix: A nightly job builds a seed snapshot: a small, anonymised dataset with realistic shapes, such as thousands of accounts with orders and edge cases, from generators or from production with personal data replaced. When a preview starts, its schema is created as a copy-on-write clone of the snapshot, which takes seconds and stores only what the preview changes. Then the migrations from the pull request's branch run on top, so the preview also tests the migration. Small fixtures load for scenarios that tests need.
steps.tradeoff: Every preview starts with the same known data, so results are repeatable and a reviewer can reproduce a bug. The snapshot has to be kept in step with the schema, and anonymisation has to be good enough that no real person can be recognised, which is a rule to test and not a hope.

steps.title: Sleep when idle, and delete on merge or after a time limit
steps.problem: Hundreds of environments stay open for days while someone looks at each one for a few minutes, and forgotten ones would be paid for forever.
steps.fix: Three layers. First, an environment with no requests for 30 minutes is scaled to zero, which frees its memory and keeps its disk. The next request is held by the ingress while the controller scales it back up, which takes about 20 seconds. Second, the merged or closed event deletes the namespace, its schema and its route. Third, a reaper compares the namespaces with the open pull requests every few minutes and deletes any environment whose pull request is closed or that is older than its time limit, such as 7 days after the last push, because events can be lost. Emptied nodes are removed by the cluster autoscaler.
steps.tradeoff: The bill follows what is used, not what exists, and nothing leaks for long. The first visit after a sleep is slow, a time limit can delete an environment someone still wants (a label on the pull request can extend it), and the reaper needs careful safeguards so that it never deletes anything but previews.

steps.title: Isolate secrets, quotas and the network
steps.problem: A preview runs code that nobody has reviewed yet, next to hundreds of others, so a bug or a malicious branch can read secrets, flood the cluster or reach other environments.
steps.fix: Each namespace gets a resource quota and limits on CPU, memory, storage and the number of objects, so a leaking preview is stopped alone. A default-deny network policy blocks traffic between namespaces and allows only the shared services. Credentials are created per environment, short-lived, scoped to its own schema and prefixes, and fetched from a secrets manager. Previews never hold production secrets, and run in a separate cluster and cloud account from production. Pull requests from forks do not get secrets until a maintainer approves them.
steps.tradeoff: A bad branch can only hurt itself, and a leak from a preview reaches nothing of value. The quotas have to be sized so normal previews fit, and per-environment credentials add a step to creation, as well as a rule to clean them up on deletion.

failures.scenario: The close event is lost when the pull request is merged
failures.impact: The environment keeps running, and since nobody knows about it, it is paid for until someone notices.
failures.answer: The reaper does not rely on events. Every few minutes it lists the preview namespaces and the open pull requests and deletes any namespace without a matching open pull request. Each namespace carries labels with its pull request number and creation time, so the check is cheap. The event gives fast cleanup and the sweep gives certainty.

failures.scenario: Forty developers open or update pull requests on Monday morning
failures.impact: The cluster runs out of room, new previews wait in the pending state, and the first impression of the platform is a spinner.
failures.answer: The autoscaler adds nodes, which takes a couple of minutes, so creation requests are queued and the status on the pull request says so. Meanwhile the least recently used sleeping and idle environments make room, and new ones are limited to a number of simultaneous creations. Common images are cached on the nodes to shorten the start.

failures.scenario: A preview has a memory leak
failures.impact: Without limits it consumes the memory of its node and the neighbours are evicted, so other people's reviews fail at random.
failures.answer: The namespace quota and the limits on each container cap it at about 4 GB, and the platform kills only that container when it goes over. The status on the pull request reports the out-of-memory restarts, so the author sees the cause. Other previews never notice.

failures.scenario: A branch from a fork prints every environment variable
failures.impact: Anyone could open a pull request that exfiltrates the credentials in its environment.
failures.answer: Previews of untrusted forks are not built until a maintainer approves them, and they get no secrets beyond their own scoped, short-lived ones for an isolated schema. Outbound traffic is limited by network policy, and nothing in a preview can reach production. The worst a malicious branch can read is test data.

alternatives.title: The unit of isolation

options.name: A namespace in a shared cluster
options.pro: Seconds to create, cheap, and many fit on a node
options.con: Weaker isolation, which needs quotas and network policies

options.name: A cluster or virtual cluster per pull request
options.pro: Strong isolation and full freedom, even for cluster-level changes
options.con: Minutes to create and much more overhead

options.name: A virtual machine per pull request
options.pro: Simple to understand and close to production
options.con: Slow to create and expensive to leave running

alternatives.pick: A namespace per pull request, with a separate cluster for previews. Use virtual clusters only for changes to the platform itself.

alternatives.title: Where the data comes from

options.name: The shared staging database
options.con: Previews interfere with each other and migrations clash

options.name: A copy-on-write clone of an anonymised snapshot
options.pro: Fast, repeatable, safe, and tests migrations

options.name: A copy of production
options.con: Slow, costly, and exposes personal data

alternatives.pick: A clone of an anonymised snapshot, plus small fixtures.

alternatives.title: How a preview is addressed

options.name: A subdomain per pull request
options.pro: Works with absolute links, cookies and the root path, so apps need no changes
options.con: Needs a wildcard certificate and cookie care

options.name: A path prefix such as /pr-482/
options.con: Many applications break when they are not at the root of a site

alternatives.pick: A subdomain, under a dedicated preview domain that is not the production domain.

alternatives.title: How cost is controlled

options.name: A time limit only
options.con: Environments run when nobody is looking, and some are deleted too early

options.name: Sleep when idle plus delete on merge plus a time limit
options.pro: Cost follows use, and nothing leaks
options.con: Slow first visit and more moving parts

alternatives.pick: All three. Sleep for the cost, delete on merge for tidiness, and the time limit as a safety net.

roles.label: People
roles.description: Developers who push and reviewers who open the link.

roles.label: Routing
roles.description: The wildcard entry point that sends each host name to its environment.

roles.label: Events
roles.description: Pull request events on their way to the controller.

roles.label: Controller and apps
roles.description: The controller, the reaper and the running environments.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Shared services, seed data, secrets and quotas.

quiz.question: A company opens about 60 pull requests a day, and the product is a dozen services plus a database. Reviewers want a running copy of each branch within about a minute, and hundreds of copies may exist at once. Which unit of isolation fits?
options: A namespace per pull request in one shared preview cluster, with quotas and network policies.
A virtual machine per pull request, cloned from a production image, which gives full isolation but takes about 10 minutes to boot and is billed all month.
A dedicated cluster per pull request, which gives complete freedom even for cluster-level changes but takes minutes to create and has heavy fixed overhead.
One shared staging environment where branches deploy in turn, with a bot that queues the deploys and tells reviewers whose branch is live.
quiz.explanation: A namespace is a cheap boundary for names, permissions and quotas, and applying templates to it takes seconds, so hundreds can coexist. Virtual machines and clusters are too slow and costly per branch. A single staging slot makes branches wait and hides a branch as soon as another replaces it.

quiz.question: 120 previews run at once. The production database is 2 TB and holds customer data. Each preview needs realistic data, its own database state, and a start time of seconds. Which approach fits?
options: Restore the latest production backup into each preview and mask the personal columns in the application code before anyone opens it.
Point all previews at the one shared staging database and let each test run clean up the rows that it created afterwards.
Mount a read-only replica of production under every preview and keep any writes in memory so nothing persists after the preview ends.
Give each preview a copy-on-write clone of a nightly anonymised snapshot, then run the branch's migrations on top, so it stores only what it changes.
quiz.explanation: A clone of a small anonymised snapshot starts in seconds, shares unchanged data, and holds no real customers. Restoring 2 TB 120 times takes hours and costs 240 TB, and masking in application code still leaves personal data in the copy. A shared staging database lets previews interfere with each other and clash on migrations.

quiz.question: A pull request is merged while the source host's webhook service is down, so the 'closed' event never arrives. Three weeks later the cloud bill shows 40 namespaces whose pull requests were merged long ago. What design prevents this?
options: Make webhook delivery more reliable with signed retries and a dead-letter queue on the receiving side, so that a close event can never be lost in transit.
Scale every preview to zero after 30 minutes without requests and delete its namespace at the same time, since nobody is using it any more.
Keep the close event for fast cleanup, and add a reaper that every few minutes compares preview namespaces with open pull requests and deletes orphans.
Give every preview a hard 24 hour lifetime from creation and delete it automatically, whatever the state of its pull request.
quiz.explanation: Events give fast cleanup but can be lost, so a sweep that compares what exists with what should exist gives certainty. Better retries still cannot promise delivery during an outage on the sender's side. A fixed 24 hour lifetime deletes environments reviewers still need, and deleting after idleness confuses sleeping with finishing.
